title: Linked lists
summary: Follow a chain of linked nodes, just like a treasure trail. Visit three values, stop at the end, and see how links differ from indexes.
introduction: A treasure clue points to the next clue. You follow the trail one clue at a time. A linked list holds items this way: each little box points to the next box.
learningObjectives: Explain nodes, links, and the head of a list
Visit every node without losing the first link
Recognize an empty list and the end of a chain

blocks.text: A **node** is a small box that holds a value and a link to the next node. A link is a reference to another box. C and C++ call such an address a pointer.
The **head** points to the first node. The final node has an empty next link, written null, NULL, nullptr, or None in these languages.
This is a **singly linked list**: each node links forward once. Unlike an array, it does not let us jump straight to item number 20. We must follow the links from the head.

items: Build a last node holding 9 with no next node.
Build a node holding 6 that links to 9, then a head node holding 3 that links to 6.
Set current to the head. Print 3, then move current to its next node.
Print 6 and then 9. Stop when current has no node.

blocks.text: Choose one tab. All six programs do the same task and print the same result. JavaScript can run here. The other languages need the separate local tools in [Language setup](/tutorials/data-structures-algorithms/language-setup).

blocks.text: Each value prints once because current moves forward after each print. The head still points to 3. The C and C++ nodes are local variables that remain alive for this whole walk; these examples do not allocate memory by hand.
Check the small and tricky cases
An empty list has an empty head link, so the loop runs zero times. A one-node list prints once, then follows an empty link and stops.
A cycle is a link that goes back to an earlier node. This simple walk assumes there is no cycle. A cycle would make it repeat forever.
Walking n nodes takes O(n) time. Adding a node after a node you already have can take O(1) link changes. Finding that place first can still take O(n).

items: Change only the middle value from 6 to 8.
The three lines become 3, 8, and 9. Changing a value does not change where the links lead.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Remember to move current to current.next. Also keep a separate current variable so you do not lose the head while walking.
